Proposal: U.S. Fertility and Age at First Birth

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To the BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026
From Yibing (Janice) Jiang
November 18, 2026

For my final project, I will examine U.S. fertility from two perspectives:

  1. How has the U.S. total fertility rate changed since 1960, and when has its trend differed from Canada’s?

  2. Among U.S. women aged 40-59 who have had at least two deliveries resulting in a live birth, how does the number of such deliveries vary with age at first birth?

Vignette 1. U.S. fertility trends in comparison with Canada

I will use the dslabs::gapminder dataset, which contains annual country-level fertility estimates compiled by Gapminder. The U.S. and Canada both have fertility estimates from 1960 to 2015. Each observation represents one country in one year. The outcome is the total fertility rate, expressed in births per woman. It summarizes the fertility a woman would experience if she passed through her reproductive years at that year’s age-specific birth rates. Gapminder dataset documentation

I will visualize the two countries’ annual rates and summarize the change in each country by decade. I will also calculate the annual difference between the U.S. and Canadian rates to identify when the gap widened or narrowed. Canada serves as a reference for interpreting the U.S. trend. For example, a decline of similar magnitude in both countries would tell a different demographic story from a decline confined to the United States.

The total fertility rate is a continuous outcome. Calendar year will be recorded numerically, and country will be coded as U.S. or Canada. I will check for missing fertility estimates and calculate annual between-country differences only for years with observations in both countries. Any missing years will be reported without interpolation. This vignette will describe population trends over time. Its comparisons will remain descriptive, with no confounder-adjusted causal interpretation.

Vignette 2. Age at first birth and subsequent reproductive history

I will use NHANESraw from the NHANES R package, pooling the 2009-2010 and 2011-2012 cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Each observation represents one participant. The target population for this analysis is U.S. civilian, noninstitutionalized women aged 40-59 who have had at least two deliveries resulting in a live birth. My exposure is age at first live birth (Age1stBaby), grouped as under 20, 20-24, 25-29, and 30 or older. My outcome is the number of deliveries resulting in a live birth by the time of interview (nBabies). A twin delivery counts once. The questionnaire routes women with one such delivery past the first-birth-age question, so I will restrict this analysis to women with at least two. A preliminary check identified 1,172 women aged 40-59 with both measures available. NHANES dataset documentation · CDC reproductive health questionnaire

The outcome, nBabies, is a discrete count of deliveries resulting in a live birth. For each age-at-first-birth group, I will report the sample size and estimate the survey-weighted mean outcome with a 95% confidence interval, accounting for the survey strata, clusters, and pooled-cycle weights. I will exclude participants with missing exposure or outcome information and report the number excluded at each step. The adjusted analysis will use participants with complete information on all model variables.

I will also use survey-weighted linear regression to estimate adjusted differences in mean delivery counts across age-at-first-birth groups, using ages 20-24 as the reference group. Before examining these associations, I will specify age at interview, race/ethnicity (Race1), and survey cycle as adjustment variables. Age captures differences in birth cohort and the duration of observed reproductive history. Race/ethnicity represents social and historical circumstances that may relate to both reproductive timing and subsequent births, while survey cycle accounts for differences between the two survey periods. I will examine model diagnostics and interpret the estimates as adjusted associations within the eligible population. As a supplementary analysis, I will repeat the descriptive comparisons separately for women aged 40-49 and 50-59.

Interpretation and limitations

The two vignettes address different time scales. Gapminder describes fertility in a given calendar year, while NHANES records births accumulated over an individual woman’s life. I will interpret the NHANES results as associations within the eligible group. Family preferences and socioeconomic circumstances may influence both when a woman first gives birth and how many births follow. Overall, the analyses will describe how U.S. fertility changed and how reproductive histories differ among mothers, while keeping those two conclusions distinct.

Restricting the NHANES analysis to women with at least two deliveries resulting in a live birth conditions the sample on the outcome and may alter the observed association. The findings will therefore apply specifically to this selected group, with limited generalizability to all U.S. women or all mothers.
